title: What determines the attainable speed and first instability of a tensile crack?
summary: A tensile crack need not approach one universal speed limit: material response, dimensionality, disorder and process-zone physics can select different speed branches and instabilities.

statement.lead: For a stated constitutive law, fracture/process-zone law, geometry and disorder, a smooth dynamic crack must satisfy energy balance and remain dynamically stable. Schematically,
equations: v_{\rm att}=\sup\{v:\text{ stable tensile-crack state exists}\},\qquad v_{\rm inst}=\inf\{v:\text{ selected smooth branch loses stability}\}.
statement.after: The open target is to derive the attainable branch, first instability, and selected post-instability mode from mechanics rather than impose a universal scalar crack-speed ceiling.

why: Dynamic fracture controls catastrophic failure under impact, shock, blast, fragmentation and rapid loading, where crack speed and instability can change failure mode within microseconds.
Experiments show microbranching, oscillatory instability, trans-Rayleigh or supershear propagation, and spall-like separation in different regimes, so onset alone is not enough.
A predictive theory would connect measurable material and geometric parameters to attainable crack speeds, the first instability, and the post-instability fracture mode.
scope: Primary target: rapidly propagating tensile cracks under Mode-I-dominated loading, with the bulk constitutive response and fracture/process-zone law declared explicitly.
Two- and three-dimensional regimes must be distinguished because crack-front waves, microbranching and disorder introduce genuinely three-dimensional physics.
Mixed-mode fracture, fragmentation and fully developed post-branching dynamics are extensions rather than assumptions hidden inside one universal law.

boundary.text: Classical dynamic fracture mechanics provides the moving-crack fields and makes the Rayleigh speed a distinguished endpoint of the conventional smooth sub-Rayleigh Mode-I LEFM branch.
Experiments showed decades ago that real brittle cracks can destabilize through microbranching well below that endpoint.
Suppressing three-dimensional microbranching in thin gels reveals a distinct high-speed oscillatory instability tied to an intrinsic nonlinear near-tip length scale.

Supershear tensile cracks have now been observed directly in strongly nonlinear materials, and continuum models show that geometric nonlinearity can support transonic/supershear branches in declared settings.
Recent three-dimensional and mode-selection studies show that disorder, branching and alternative separation modes can determine an effective limiting speed or redirect the failure pathway.

2026 experiments in highly entangled hydrogels and recent peridynamic computations further reinforce that attainable speed and first instability are material/process-zone dependent. No general branch-selection/stability theory was identified that predicts all of these regimes from independently specified inputs.

settle: Derive a stability/selection theory that predicts the first dynamic instability and attainable crack branch from independently measurable material, process-zone, geometric and disorder parameters.
Provide a mechanics-based criterion distinguishing sub-Rayleigh, trans-Rayleigh, supershear, branching, oscillatory and spall-like regimes within its declared validity class.
A counterexample or no-go result showing that a proposed reduced set of parameters cannot determine branch selection would also sharpen the boundary.

progress.title: New high-speed hydrogel experiments expose another material regime
progress.text: Experiments report strongly rate- and material-dependent high-speed fracture with unconventional branching, reinforcing the branch-selection framing.

progress.title: Tensile failure shown to switch among distinct dynamic modes
progress.text: Crack-like, supershear-like and spall-like separation modes were analyzed within one tensile-loading framework.

progress.title: Nonlinearity and disorder sharpen the modern speed-limit picture
progress.text: Continuum supershear branches and disorder-controlled 3D limiting behavior were demonstrated in complementary settings.
